ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
- The Trial Court committed reversible error as a matter of law when it granted the Defendant-Appellee's, State Auto Insurance Companies' ("State Auto"), Motion for Summary Judgment in light of the fact the Plaintiff-Appellants' ("Siemientkowskis"), submitted valid and timely claims of malicious prosecution and libel covered under their Homeowners Policy.
II. The Trial Court erred when it granted State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment after being presented with irrefutable evidence based upon Attorney John Lind's testimony, as a witness under oath, that Ohio Farmers voluntarily incurred additional legal costs to defend itself against malicious prosecution and damage to Ohio Farmers' reputation.
III. The Trial Court erred when it granted State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment after being presented with irrefutable evidence that the trial judge at the 2323.51 Hearing and the Eighth District Court of Appeals upon appeal upheld the award Ohio Farmers' voluntarily brought upon itself to defend against allegations of malicious prosecution and damage to reputation.
IV. The Trial Court committed reversible error as a matter of law when it granted State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment as to all of the Siemientkowski's claims when State Auto never addressed the Siemientkowski's claim of bad faith in its Motion for Summary Judgment, the determination of bad faith lying within the province of the jury.
V. The Trial Court erred when it granted State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment before the completion of the discovery process prior to the scheduled cutoff date of November 1, 2005.
VI. The Trial Court committed reversible error in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment when issues of material fact exist to be decided by a jury.
VII. The Trial Court committed reversible error in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment on the disputed allegation the Siemientkowskis failed to notify State Auto in a timely fashion.
VIII. The Trial Court committed reversible error in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment on the disputed allegation the Siemientkowskis intentionally and voluntarily incurred losses.
IX. The Trial Court committed reversible error in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment based on State Auto's interpretation that any violation of R.C. 2323.51 is a violation of the "Penal Code"
1

X. The Trial Court committed reversible error in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment as to the jury question of whether or not State Auto breached its contract with the Siemientkowskis.
XI. The Trial Court committed reversible error in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment, in the absence of a written memorandum from the trial judge at the 2323.51 Hearing, that all or a part of the award of attorney fees were based on Ohio Farmers' allegations of malicious prosecution and/or damage to reputation.
APPELLATE JURISDICTION
The Appellants, Ronald J. Siemientkowski and Sara L. Siemientkowski, seek reversal of the Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court Order dated October 21, 2005 and journalized on October 25, 2005 granting Appellee's, State Auto Insurance Companies, Motion for Summary Judgment.
Accordingly, The Eighth District Court of Appeals has jurisdiction over Appellants' Appeal pursuant to Ohio Civil Code §2505.03. On October 21, 2005 the Honorable Judge Nancy R. McDonnell granted judgment to Appellee State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment, a final order subject to appeal.
STATEMENT OF ISSUES FOR REVIEW
On October 21, 2005 and journalized on October 25, 2005, the lower court granted State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment. See Exhibit 2.
The lower court erred in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment as a matter of law when it was clear from the Siemientkowskis' Homeowners Policy, the Siemientkowskis had absolute coverage against claims of malicious prosecution and libel under the contract between the parties. See Exhibit 3. The lower court ignored
2

convincing evidence that Ohio Farmers voluntarily incurred additional legal costs to defend itself against malicious prosecution and damage to reputation. State Auto has absolute liability as set forth in the terms of the Homeowners Policy under its Special Coverage Endorsement. Coverage for malicious prosecution and damage to reputation under the Homeowners Policy is absolute and the determination of whether the Siemientkowskis claims are covered lie with the jury.
The issue of bad faith is a tort claim to be decided by a jury precluding the granting of summary judgment on the issue of bad faith by the trial court. In an action alleging bad faith denial of insurance coverage, the Siemientkowskis are entitled to discover claim file materials containing attorney-client communications related to the issue of coverage that were created prior to the denial of coverage.
Many fact questions for the jury precluded summary judgment by the trial court, that is, the disputed allegations of whether the Siemientkowskis filed a timely claim, intentionally and voluntarily incurred losses, if State Auto is liable for coverage of part or all of the attorney fees awarded to Ohio Farmers, etc.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
On May 24, 2004 within the terms of their Homeowners Policy, the Siemientkowskis submitted to State Auto a claim for $29,455.74 and other costs to cover a judgment awarded to Ohio Farmers Insurance Company against the Plaintiffs on May 5, 2004 and the Siemientkowskis' costs to defend themselves. See Exhibit 4. The judgment against the Siemientkowskis included Ohio Farmers' voluntarily incurred legal expenses, money Ohio Farmers admitted was well worth the expense, for what
3

Ohio Farmers viewed and testified under oath as to the Siemientkowskis' acts of malicious prosecution and damage to Ohio Farmers' reputation.
The personal liability incurred by the Plaintiffs was neither expected nor intended. The Plaintiffs submitted their legitimate claim to State Auto as provided for under their Homeowners Policy on May 24, 2004. Instead of processing Plaintiffs claim in good faith, State Auto, through Kip Reader of Ulmer Berne LLP, issued a threat through the United States mail on June 3, 2004 of additional financial ruin to the Plaintiffs. See Exhibit 5. After attempts to file a claim with State Auto failed, the Siemientkowskis filed a complaint in Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court on May 27, 2005 against State Auto alleging breach of contract, failure to exercise good faith in the processing of a claim and bad faith denial of insurance coverage.
Lacking any good reason, the lower court on October 21, 2005 granted State .Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment which was journalized on October 25, 2005 without a Memorandum of Opinion. On October 31, 2005 the Siemientkowskis filed a Request for a Memorandum of Opinion from the lower Court and was denied on December 6, 2005. Exhibit 8.
Based upon the Siemientkowskis arguments and exhibits contained in their Opposition to State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment and the Homeowners Policy, the lower court had no legitimate basis in law or fact for granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment.
4

STATEMENT OF FACTS
On May 3, 2004 a hearing was held to consider Ohio Farmers' Motion for Attorney Fees as Sanctions for Frivolous Conduct. Frivolous conduct was and is not covered by the Homeowners' Policy issued to the Siemientkowskis by State Auto.
State Auto argues that the Siemientkowskis failed to file a claim against its Homeowners Policy depriving State Auto of the right to defend the Siemientkowskis at that 2323.51 hearing or to negotiate a settlement before a judgment and therefore the Siemientkowskis forfeited their right to make a claim under the Homeowners Policy.
Prior to the hearing on May 3, 2004, the Siemientkowskis had no claim against their Homeowners Policy for malicious prosecution, abuse of process, libel, slander or defamation of character. It wasn't until the hearing when John K. Lind provided sworn testimony under oath that their claim arose. See Exhibit 6, Transcript of Proceedings.
John Lind, Esq. representing Ohio Farmers Insurance Companies, at the 2323.51 Hearing on May 3rd, 2004 before Judge Eileen Gallagher, Siemientkowski, et al. v. Moreland Homes. See Exhibit 6, Transcript pp 15, 16, 26 describes Ohio Farmers' losses in the following manner:
... it's abuse of process or malicious prosecution under 2323.51.
... which outlines the elements of abuse of process and malicious prosecution.
... Robb v. Chagrin Lagoons Yacht Club. The citiation is 75 Ohio State 3d 264 which outlines the elements of abuse of process and malicious prosecution.
... and the reputation is worth the money to defend.
State Auto's Home Owner Policy issued to the Siemientkowskis clearly states:
5

The definition of "bodily injury" is amended to include personal injury. Personal injury means injury arising out of one or more of the following offenses:
1. false arrest, detention or imprisonment, or malicious prosecution;
2. libel, slander or defamation of character; or
3. invasion of privacy, wrongful eviction or wrongful entry.
Special Coverage Endorsement. The Home Defender Homeowners Policy. State Auto Insurance Company. See Special Coverage Endorsement, Part A - Change in Definition contained in and part of the Homeowners Policy. Exhibit 3 which was previously filed as a complete policy document attached to Plaintiffs' Original Complaint and also as an exhibit to State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment.
Ronald J. Siemientkowski entered Fairview Hospital on May 5, 2004 the same day that Judge Gallagher's judgment entry was journalized. Surgery to remove two fungating cancerous masses, lymph nodes and Ronald's ascending colon took place on May 11, 2004. Contrary to the mean spirited and crude remark from State Auto's attorney that the Court should view this fact as an attempt to gain sympathy and should be ignored, it is a fact and a justifiable reason why the Siemientkowskis didn't file their claim sooner. Notwithstanding this fact, the Siemientkowskis made a timely claim.
The Siemientkowskis sent a letter notifying State Auto of the then known claim for loss on May 24, 2004 giving State Auto plenty of time to participate in the appeal, process. Exhibit 4. State Auto did not write a claim rejection letter, did not elect to help in the appeals process, did not elect to negotiate a lesser judgment or call to discuss the claim but instead had their attorney send a letter to threaten the Siemientkowskis with additional financial harm if the Siemientkowskis pursued their valid homeowners' insurance claim. Exhibit 5.

0
For State Auto to maintain that it was necessary for the Siemientkowskis to have informed State Auto of the 2323.51 hearing has no merit as a claim against the Homeowners Policy did not exist at that point in time. The claim only became evident when John K. Lind, under oath, testified as to why Ohio Farmers felt justified in voluntarily running up its attorney fees.
State Auto's Homeowners Policy clearly provides coverage for the claims against the Siemientkowskis as outlined under oath by Ohio Farmers Attorney. The Hearing transcript of May 3, 2004 speaks for itself as absolute evidence that the Siemientkowskis were sanctioned for covered claims. The sworn testimony of John Lind is evidence and must be treated as evidence.
On the face of the Homeowners Policy, the Siemientkowskis have absolute coverage for malicious prosecution, libel, slander and defamation. Since this fact of State Auto's liability is in dispute, the lower court erred in granting summary judgment instead of turning the question over to the jury to decide.
Where provisions of insurance contract are reasonably susceptible to more than one interpretation, Court of Appeals must construe provision strictly against insurer and liberally in favor of insured. Auto-Owners Ins. Co. v. Brubaker, (Ohio App. 6 Dist. 1994), 93 Ohio App.3d 211, 638 N.E.2d 124. 93 Ohio App.3d 211, 638 N.E.2d 124. King v. Nationwide Ins. Co. (1988), 35 Ohio St.3d 208, 519 N.E.2d 1380,
State Auto did not present any evidence whatsoever that the Siemientkowskis knew prior to the May 3, 2004 hearing that John Lind, Attorney for Ohio Farmers Insurance Company, would be asserting against the Siemientkowskis, to justify their grossly inflated legal fees, the defense of malicious prosecution, libel, slander and defamation,

all of which are covered by State Auto's Homeowners Policy issued to and paid for by the Siemientkowskis.
State Auto presented absolutely no evidence whatsoever that the Siemientkowskis knew prior to the hearing that they had coverage and decided not to involve State Auto, and thus, the Siemientkowskis voluntarily incurred losses for which State Auto may have been able to overcome or minimize. This is a fact question for the jury and not a basis for the granting of Summary Judgment.
Without any actual proof of the Siemientkowskis culpable state of mind, it must be defined as an accident that the Siemientkowskis found themselves being sanctioned for abuse of process, malicious prosecution and damage to reputation. The state of the Siemientkowskis' mind and whether they believed they had standing to include Ohio Farmers is a fact question for the jury. The Siemientkowskis at all times believed and still believe that Ohio Farmers belonged in the Moreland Homes case.
State Auto did not address or dispute the bad faith claims in its Motion for Summary Judgment. If the lower court had any grounds to grant a summary judgment to State Auto, it should have been a partial summary judgment with the bad faith claim pending, allowing the Siemientkowskis the right to a trial by jury on the claims of bad faith.
State Auto alleged that the Siemientkowskis were not covered as they were in violation of a penal code and therefore excluded from coverage. State Auto failed to present evidence of the exact penal code violation that would exclude coverage.
If State Auto's Homeowners Policy does not cover the Siemientkowskis then the policy is fraudulent as to coverage under the special coverage endorsement for
8

malicious prosecution, libel, slander and defamation as these claims by the very nature of their elements can never withstand State Auto's definition of accident.
If State Auto's Homeowners Policy does not cover the Siemientkowskis, then the coverage under the special coverage endorsement is fraudulent and as such an insured can never successfully present a claim.
State Auto is in breach of contract, not only with the Siemientkowskis, but with all its policyholders for providing coverage for which a policy holder can never successfully present a claim.
ARGUMENT
The Appellants, Ronald J. and Sara L. Siemientkowski include as if rewritten here all their Motions and Exhibits of record which are before the lower court.
ASSIGNMENTS I, Il and III.
State Auto issued a Homeowners Policy to the Siemientkowskis which included a Special Coverage Endorsement .. See Special Coverage Endorsement, Part A - Change in Definition. Exhibit 3.
As a matter of law and fact, the Siemientkowskis have coverage under a Special Coverage Endorsement to their Homeowners Policy for
1. false arrest, detention or imprisonment, or malicious prosecution;
2. libel, slander or defamation of character; or
3. invasion of privacy, wrongful eviction or wrongful entry.
Whether the Siemientkowskis' claims against their Homeowners Policy fall under that coverage is a question for the jury and not to be disposed of by Summary Judgment.
9

It is a fact backed by irrefutable evidence that Ohio Farmers voluntarily incurred outrageous attorney fees to defend itself against the Siemientkowskis' alleged acts of malicious prosecution and damage to reputation and used these allegations in support of their frivolous claims. See Exhibit 6, Transcript.
Lind as witness, under oath, for Ohio Farmers states Ohio Farmers had meetings and decided to spend whatever it takes to defend their reputation. " ... reputation is worth the money to defend. And that's what they decided to do. I spoke to them about this. There were meetings about this." Transcript, p. 26, 1. 9- 14. Based upon Lind's testimony under oath, the Siemientkowskis were heavily sanctioned by Judge Gallagher and that decision was upheld by the Appellate Court.
State Auto had no reasonable justification in law or fact for refusing to satisfy the Siemientkowskis' claim. As a matter of fact State Auto never sent a rejection letter. Instead State Auto sent the Siemientkowskis a letter through its attorney threatening the Siemientkowski with additional financial harm.
In Sanderson v. Ohio Edison Co. (1994), 69 Ohio St.3d 582, 635 N.E.2d 19, the Supreme Court cited its holding in Willoughby Hills v. Cincinnati Ins. Co. (1984), 9 Ohio St.3d 177, 9 OBR 463, 459 N.E.2d 555. In Willoughby Hills, the court held that where the insurer's duty to defend is not apparent from the pleadings, but the allegations state a claim which is potentially or arguably within the policy coverage, or there is some doubt as to whether a theory of recovery within the policy coverage has been pled, the insurer must accept the defense of the claim. In Sanderson, the court stated that an insurer has an absolute duty to defend under certain conditions:
"An insurance policy which states that the insurer is obligated to defend in any action seeking damages payable under the policy against the insured, even where the allegations are groundless, false or fraudulent, imposes an absolute duty upon the insurer to assume the defense of the action where the complaint states a claim which is partially or arguably within policy coverage." Id.
10

State Auto cannot be granted summary judgment based on cases where attorney fees were not awarded for malicious prosecution. This case is different from all those cases State Auto is relying on as a defense because different facts exist. In this case, Ohio Farmers elected to stay in the case for two years to defend their reputation. " ... reputation is worth the money to defend. And that's what Ohio Farmers decided to do. Lind spoke to Ohio Farmers and there were meetings in which they decided to deliberately stay in a case for the sole reason to defend their reputation. The Court must recognize the testimony of John Lind, under oath admitting that he advised his client, Ohio Farmers to file an action for frivolous conduct immediately upon receipt of being sued in State Court, but Ohio Farmers had meetings ... Decided to go the expense ... To defend Ohio Farmers reputation.
ASSIGNMENTS IV AND V
State Auto's response to the Siemientkowskis' good faith and legitimate claim for damages resulting from the 2323.51 Hearing was the threat of even more sanctions. It is the normal course of business for an insurer to directly respond to its insured's claim by providing the insured with claim forms in order to learn the facts, investigate and finally make a determination. State Auto's response to the Siemientkowskis' claim goes beyond bad faith and represents an intentional failure by State Auto to perform its contractual obligation.
Please be advised that your misconduct in regard to State Auto may subject you to sanctions under provisions of Rule 11 and Ohio Revised Code § 2323.51. State Auto hereby notifies you that it reserves the right to assert a claim for sanctions at the appropriate time. See Exhibit 5, Letter dated June 3, 2004
11

Such a response to an insured by the insurer is terrifying and malicious. No insured expects to get such a response from its insurer to a legitimate claim covered under any insurance policy.
It is clear that State Auto, in bad faith, chose to intimidate the Siemientkowskis in order not to honor a valid claim against their policy. Good faith would have required some sort of civil response to a claim rather than a threat of economic damage.
Cause of action arises for tort of bad faith when insurer breaches it duty of good faith by intentionally refusing to satisfy an insured's claim where there is either no lawful basis for refusal coupled with actual knowledge of that fact or intentional failure to determine whether there was any lawful basis for such refusal. Motorists Mut. Ins. Co. v. Said, (Ohio 1992), 63 Ohio St.3d 690, 590 N.E.2d 1228,
State Auto's response to the Siemientkowskis' lawful claim against its
Homeowners Policy was malicious in nature and had no lawful basis for refusal coupled with actual knowledge of that fact. 3
State Auto had more than a fair opportunity to represent the Siemientkowskis in the appeals process but chose to threaten the Siemientkowskis instead. State Auto has no grounds whatsoever to a summary judgment based on State Auto's bad faith acts toward the Siemientkowskis for which State Auto offered no defense.
State Auto chose to threaten the Siemientkowskis with sanctions rather than assist in the appeals process or negotiate a settlement with Ohio Farmers. State Auto has no grounds to complain about the size of the judgment for which they are liable and cannot be granted a summary judgment based on their own decision not to honor their policy provisions.
In an action alleging bad faith denial of insurance coverage, the insured is entitled to discover claims file materials containing attorney-client communications
12

related to the issue of coverage that were created prior to the denial of coverage. Boone v. Vanliner Ins. Co. (2001), 91 Ohio St.3d 209. The Supreme Court held that documents showing an insurer's bad faith failure to settle should be discoverable and were not worthy of protection under the attorney-client privilege or work product doctrine. Moskovitz v. Mt. Sinai Med. Ctr. (1994), 69 Ohio St.3d 638.
As outlined and filed in their October 17, 2005 Motion to Compel, the Siemientkowskis were denied their right to discovery claim materials. The trial court erred in light of State Auto's bad faith acts to terminate discovery when it granted summary judgment to State Auto. Furthermore, the receipt of these discovery document requests were necessary for the Siemientkowskis' need and right to also amend the complaint.
ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR VI, VII, VIII, IX, X AND XI
Assignments of error VI through XI deal with genuine issues of material fact which as a matter of law precludes summary judgment. The trial court erred by granting summary judgment where there are genuine issues of material fact.
The Supreme Court of Ohio has stated:
"'Civ.R. 56(C) specifically provides that before summary judgment may be granted, it must be determined that: (1) No genuine issue as to any material fact remains to be litigated; (2) the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law; and (3) it appears from the evidence that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and viewing the evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgment is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party.' Temple v. Wean United, Inc. (1977), 50 Ohio St.2d 317, 327, 4 0.0.3d 466, 472, 364 N.E.2d 267, 274.
Moreover, ' * upon appeal from summary judgment, the reviewing court should look at the record in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion.' Campbell v. Hospitality Motor Inns, Inc. (1986), 24 Ohio
13

St.3d 54, 58, 24 OBR 135, 138, 493 N.E.2d 239, 242." Osborne v. Lyles (1992), 63 Ohio St.3d 326, 327.
There is ample evidence that the Siemientkowskis notified State Auto "as soon as is practical" of a claim. State Auto outlined the insureds' duties after a loss and the Siemientkowskis were in compliance with the terms of the policy. Yet, State Auto claims it was prejudiced by the Siemientkowskis' failure to comply with the policy's notice condition. State Auto was given ample time to negotiate a settlement and/or to represent the Siemientkowskis on appeal. The question of whether State Auto was disadvantaged by the timeliness of the Siemientkowskis' filing of their claim under their policy provisions is a genuine issue of material fact for determination by the jury.
State Auto failed to show that injury caused by the Siemientkowskis itself was expected or intended in order to avoid coverage on basis of exclusion for expected or intentional injuries; it is not insured's intentional act or conduct which controls, but whether insured intended injury to result. Physicians Ins. Co. of Ohio v. Swanson, (Ohio 1991), 58 Ohio St.3d 189, 569 N.E.2d 906.
The Siemientkowskis never dreamt in their wildest dreams that they would be punished for initiating a claim in good faith against Ohio Farmers. The Siemientkowskis never dreamt that anyone would view their actions as malicious prosecution, libel, slander and defamation of character let alone further punish the Siemientkowskis by awarding outrageous attorney fees for voluntary expenses incurred by a defendant that spent that money admitting that it was well worth the expense.
In order for exclusion for intentional acts to apply, insurer must show not only that insured intended act, but also that insured intended to cause harm or injury. Physicians Ins. Co. of Ohio v. Swanson, (Ohio 1991), 58 Ohio St.3d 189, 569 N.E.2d 906.
14

No where in its pleadings did State Auto show by clear and convincing evidence that the Siemientkowskis intended to cause harm or injury to Ohio Farmers by naming Ohio Farmers as a defendant in Siemientkowski v. Moreland Homes.
Likewise, in Farmers Ins. Group v. Sessions (1980), 100 Idaho 914, 607 P.2d 422, the court held that for an exclusion for injuries intentionally caused to operate, the insurance company must demonstrate that the insured acted " * * * for the purpose of causing injury in the person or property in which it resulted." Physicians Ins. Co. of Ohio v. Swanson, (Ohio 1991), 58 Ohio St.3d 189, 569 N.E.2d 918, 607 P.2d at 426. In so holding, the court rejected the insurer's argument that the policy requires nothing more than an intentional act for the exclusion to operate. The court stated as follows:
" * * Such an interpretation would radically alter the scope of insurance company liability. On an exclusion such as this one, the company would have no liability for the baseball intentionally thrown which accidentally breaks the neighbor's window, the intentional lane change which forces another driver into the ditch, or the intentionally started trash fire which spreads to the adjacent lot. Countless other examples are imaginable, in all of which the insurance company could rely on such an exclusion to avoid liability because the course of conduct of the insured involved intentional acts. * " Id. at 917, 607 P.2d at 425.
In Colonial Penn Ins. Co. v. Hart (1982), 162 Ga.App. 333, 291 S.E.2d 410, the evidence presented at trial showed that the insured had fired at a vandal in an attempt to frighten him. The court framed the issue as follows: " * * * the issue in the instant case was not whether Mr. Rice intentionally fired the shotgun. This fact is uncontroverted. Rather, '[t]he only issue ... was whether the [bodily injury] was "either expected or intended from the standpoint of [Mr. Rice]" * * * ' Transamerica Ins. Co. v. Thrift-Mart, 159 Ga.App. 874, 881 (285 S.E.2d 566) (1981)." (Emphasis sic.) Id. 162 Ga.App. at 335, 291 S.E.2d at 412. The court upheld the jury's finding that the injury to the vandal was not intentional, and thus the exclusion was inapplicable.
It is an uncontroverted fact that the Siemientkowskis named Ohio Farmers as a defendant in Siemientkowski v. Moreland Homes. The issue here is whether by the intentional naming of Ohio Farmers as a Defendant, the Siemientkowskis expected or
15

intended from their standpoint to cause harm or injury resulting from frivolous conduct, malicious prosecution or damage to reputation of Ohio Farmers.
Whether the Siemientkowskis intentional act of naming Ohio Farmers as a defendant was for the express purpose of causing harm or injury is a genuine material fact for determination by the jury.
State Auto has not supplied any evidence that the Siemientkowskis violated any "Penal Code or Codes" and is without merit and therefore cannot operate to award summary judgment.
Based on the Siemientkowskis absolute coverage under their Homeowners Policy it was a genuine issue of material fact for the jury to determine the question of State Auto's breach of contract.
Absent a written memorandum from the trial judge at the 2323.51 hearing it was a genuine issue of material fact for the jury to determine when liability ended for frivolous conduct and liability began for malicious prosecution and damage to reputation to determine actual liability of State Auto for damages under the Siemientkowskis' Homeowners Policy.
The trial court erred by granting summary judgment where there are so many genuine issues of material fact to be determined by the jury.
CONCLUSION
State Auto has failed to provide any evidence for which summary judgment could be granted. The Siemientkowskis request this Honorable Court to overturn the lower
16

court's decision in granting State Auto's Motion for Summary judgment and to return this case for further proceedings.
State Auto failed to offer any defense for the claims of bad faith in their Motion for Summary Judgment and therefore cannot be granted Summary Judgment on the issue of bad faith. State Auto through its bad faith conduct failed to mitigate its liability under the Homeowners Policy coverage and intentionally inflicted emotional distress upon its insureds.
Appelllants further request this Honorable Court to:
(1) overturn the lower court's decision granting State Auto's Motion for Summary Judgment and send the case back to the lower court for a trial by jury;
(2) send the case back to the lower court for a trial by jury on the Siemientkowskis' bad faith claims against State Auto;
(3) compel State Auto to supply requested discovery; and,
(4) grant the Appellants the cost in filing ($125.00) and reasonable costs (to be determined) associated with the bringing of this appeal.
